name: Dandelion extract
lead: Dandelion extract is a preparation from the leaves, roots or flowers of Taraxacum officinale, the common dandelion, a perennial of the daisy family (Asteraceae) native to Eurasia.[1] The leaves, flowers and roots are used as food and in herbal medicine, and extracts are sold as teas, capsules and tinctures.[1]

The plant has a long reputation as a diuretic. Wikipedia notes that this property is attributed to its high potassium content, that the leaves have been used as a diuretic in traditional Chinese medicine for roughly 2,000 years, and that French and English folk names ('pissenlit', 'piss-a-bed') refer to it. A 2009 study described 'promising' results while calling for further research.[1][2] In appearance communities it is discussed as a way to reduce 'water weight' and facial bloating.[15][16]

No published trial has tested dandelion extract for facial puffiness. Most laboratory research in the sources reviewed concerns antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer and animal-nutrition effects in cells and animals rather than humans.[3][4][6]

Mild diuretic, digestive and liver remedy[1][2]

paras: Traditional uses in European, North American and Chinese herbal medicine include diuresis, digestion and liver complaints; Chinese medicine also uses Taraxacum mongolicum for breast abscess and mastitis.[1][5] In appearance contexts, dandelion root or leaf is mentioned in forum discussions as an herbal diuretic for water retention and bloating, as well as in 'liver support' stacks used by people on anabolic steroids.[15][16][17]

The diuretic effect is traditionally attributed to the plant's potassium content.[1] Laboratory work reports antioxidant activity and inhibition of inflammatory signalling in cell and animal models, including macrophage and zebrafish studies and oxidative-stress models in bovine mammary cells.[3][6][11] Chemical constituents of the root include the inulin-containing polysaccharides and a serine proteinase in the latex.[1]

Dandelion is a member of the Asteraceae (Compositae) family, and contact allergy to Compositae plants is a recognised clinical entity studied with patch testing and described in people with atopic dermatitis.[13][14] Herbal products vary in quality and composition. Interaction data in the sources reviewed are limited.
No studies found on dandelion extract for facial puffiness or depuffing.

Related research: Wikipedia cites a 2009 study that reported promising diuretic effects of dandelion leaf and called for further work.[1] Registered human trials include a trial of dandelion in obese perimenopausal women (n=120),[7] a small trial of dandelion juice in hand eczema (n=4),[8] and bloating-supplement trials in which dandelion may be one of several ingredients.[9] Other published work consists of in vitro, animal and veterinary studies, such as antioxidant effects in cells, dairy cows and fish, and in vitro gallstone dissolution.[4][6][10]

timeline.event: Carl Linnaeus names the species Leontodon taraxacum; the current genus name Taraxacum follows.[1]
A study notes promising diuretic properties of dandelion leaf.[1]

lore.intro: On T Nation, dandelion root is occasionally mentioned as an herbal diuretic for water retention and as a component of liver-support supplement lists.[15][16]

claims.claim: Dandelion root or leaf works as an herbal diuretic that reduces water weight and bloating.
claims.believers: A forum member advised that dandelion root, an herbal diuretic, could help a person whose weight fluctuated through water retention.[15]
claims.experts: The traditional diuretic reputation is long-standing, and one 2009 study reported promising results, but further studies were called for; no trial has tested it for facial puffiness.[1]

claims.believers: Users discussing steroid use suggest dandelion root extract, tea and similar herbs for liver and kidney support.[16][17]
claims.experts: Laboratory research reports antioxidant effects in rat liver injury and cell models, but the sources reviewed contain no human trial of liver protection.[12][6]
